### RNA-sequencing preprocessing

Sequencing reads were first trimmed for adaptor sequences using trim_galore (Krueger, 2020, --quality 20, --paired, --overlap 10, adaptors AAAAAAAAAA and GTACTCTGCGTTGATACCACTGCTTCCGCGGACAGGCGTGTAGATCT). We first generated an initial alignment to the Bengalese finch genome (lonStrDom2, GCF_005870125.1) using STAR v2.7.8a (STARsolo mode, default parameters, --outFilterIntronMotifs RemoveNoncanonical) (Dobin et al., 2013). To better annotate the 3’ UTRs of Bengalese finch gene models, we identified transcript 3’ ends by assembling transcripts using these initial alignments and the RNA-seq assembler Stringtie (Kovaka et al., 2019) (--fr -m 100). These Stringtie models were then intersected with the NCBI Bengalese finch transcriptome (lonStrDom2, GCF_005870125.1). New Stringtie exons were filtered by same-strandedness to the intersected reference genes, a minimal expression level (at least 10% of expression max for a given gene), and at least within 10 kilobases from the 3’ end of the gene. 3’ UTRs of the reference transcriptome were extended out to these new exons. Reads were then re-aligned to this extended transcriptome using the ‘bus’ subcommand from kallisto v0.46.1 Bray et al., 2016; Melsted et al., 2021 followed by barcode error correction using bustools v0.39.3 ‘correct,’ sorting using ‘sort,’ and read counting using ‘count.’.

### Differential expression analysis

Gene-sample count matrices were filtered to remove lowly expressed genes, defined as having a total number of reads across samples less than the number of samples divided by eight (the number of brain regions assayed). For each sample we also calculated the ‘cellular detection rate (CDR)’ or the number of genes detected in a given sample, previously shown to substantially influence differential expression analysis on single-cell RNA-sequencing samples (Finak et al., 2015). Low-quality samples were defined as having a CDR of less than 30% of the total number of genes in the reference annotation (18,674 genes). Normalization factors were calculated using the function calcNormFactors from the R package edgeR v3.31.4 and the ‘TMMwsp’ method. ### Network analysis

We used the R package MEGENA (Multiscale Clustering of Geometrical Network, v1.3.7) to identify modules of genes with correlated expression across SLCR-seq data (Song and Zhang, 2015). Low-quality samples were removed by retaining samples with cellular detection rates above 0.42. Samples expression values were normalized using normalization factors calculated as described in ‘Differential expression analysis’(calcNormFactors and the ‘TMMwsp’ method) and then log-transformed with a pseudocount of 1. Samples were then split by brain region. To remove batch effects contributed by which pool a given sample was in, we used the function ComBat (Johnson et al., 2007) from the R package sva v3.40.0. For each brain region, we then selected the top 2000 variable genes as defined using the Seurat function FindVariableFeatures v4.0.4 and the ‘vst’ method. Signed Pearson correlations between every pair of genes were then calculated using the function calculate.correlation from MEGENA, which calculates false discovery rates by permutation (50 permutations). Correlations with an FDR less than 0.05 were retained. We passed these pairwise correlations to function calculate.PFN to generate a more sparse network that retains information edges using the MEGENA Planar Filtered Network algorithm. Module detection was then performed on this filtered network using the function do.MEGENA.

To identify modules associated with behavioral features, we calculated the average of log-transformed estimates for a given coefficient across genes in a given module. To identify modules with greater (or lesser) than expected fold-changes, for each module we randomly selected the same number of genes and averaged their log-transformed coefficient estimates 100 times. Modules that had averages less than 1% or greater than 99% of this null distribution were considered significant. Hub genes were designated using the approach defined in MEGENA. For each module, the link weights of the planar filtered network were permuted 100 times to generate a set of random networks. Within-module connectivities, defined as the sum of link weights with each other gene in a gene’s module, were calculated for each gene in each random network. The p-value was calculated as the probability of finding within-module connectivity values from this null distribution equal to or greater than the observed within-module connectivity. These p-values were then adjusted using the Benjamini-Hochberg method and genes with adjusted p-values less than 0.05 were designated hub genes.

To compute gene module memberships, eigengenes were first determined for each module using the R package WGCNA v1.70–3 (Langfelder and Horvath, 2008), and function moduleEigengenes then the Pearson correlation was computed between each module eigengene and each gene. Module preservation statistics were calculated using the WGCNA function modulePreservation (Langfelder et al., 2011).

### Gene set enrichment analysis

Gene Ontology lists were obtained from the Molecular Signatures Database (set C5, version 7). Gene set enrichment analysis was performed using the R package fgsea v1.18.0 (Korotkevich et al., 2021). T-statistics from voom regression or gene module membership scores from MEGENA were input into the function fgseaMultilevel (minSize = 20, maxSize = 200). Resulting pathways were filtered for those with an adjusted p-value less than 0.2 and similar pathways were pruned using collapsedPathways (pval.threshold=0.01 or 0.05).

### Inter-region correlation analysis

To analyze inter-region gene correlations, we first selected in each region the 500 genes with the highest variability, computed as the variance-mean ratio of non-log expression across samples. For each gene, we calculated Pearson correlation values for each pairwise combination of brain regions, yielding region-by-region correlation matrices. To generate null distributions for each gene, we shuffled bird identities for each pairwise region-region comparison 100 times and computed Pearson correlations. We thresholded observed correlations using statistics from these shuffled distributions (correlation lesser or greater than the 2.5% or 97.5% shuffled quantiles). We calculated the across-bird expression similarity between regions as the number of thresholded correlations.

To determine if deafening alters inter-region gene expression coupling in the song system, we computed pairwise Pearson correlations for each gene between each region for hearing and deaf birds separately, then took the absolute value for each matrix. The hearing absolute correlation matrix was then subtracted from the deaf absolute correlation matrix. This procedure was repeated on 100 shuffled distributions to generate a null distribution of differential absolute correlations. Differentially correlated genes were called as those with a deaf versus hearing value less than (decorrelation) or greater than (correlation gain) extreme values of a shuffled distribution calculated for each pairwise comparison (2.5% or 97.5%, respectively).

### Cell type specificity and differential expression scores

For each gene, a specificity score was calculated as $\sumx_{n}logx_{n}/x_{n}¯$ , where $x_{n}$ is expression divided by the sum of expression across all clusters and $x_{n}¯$ is the mean of this value. Regression coefficient-cell type specificity scores were calculated by selecting differentially expressed genes (adjusted p-value <0.1) and then splitting genes by the sign of the coefficient. Scores were then computed as the dot-product between the cell type × gene specificity matrix and the gene × coefficient matrix.

### Fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH)

FISH was performed using the hairpin chain reaction system from Molecular Instruments. Birds were euthanized using isoflurane, decapitated, and debrained. Brains were flash-frozen in –70 °C dry ice-chilled isopentane for 12 s within 4 min from decapitation then stored at –80 °C. Fresh-frozen brains were cryosectioned at 16 μm onto SuperFrost slides (Fisherbrand) chilled in the cryochamber then melted onto the slide using a warmed metal dowel. Slides were then transferred to –80 °C for storage. For the FISH, slides were transferred from –80 °C to slide mailers containing cold 4% PFA and incubated for 15 min on ice. Slides were washed three times for 5 min using DEPC-treated PBS + 0.1% Tween-20, dehydrated in 50%, 70%, and two rounds of 100% ethanol for 3–5 min each round, then air dried. Slides were then transferred to a SlideMoat (Boekel Scientific) at 37 °C. 100 μL of v3 Hybridization Buffer (Molecular Instruments) was added to each slide, which were then coverslipped and incubated for 10 min at 37 °C. Meanwhile, 2 nM of each probe was added to 100 μL Hybridization Buffer and denatured at 37 °C. Pre-hybridization buffer was removed, 100 μL of probe/buffer was added, and slides were coverslipped and incubated overnight at 37 °C. The next day, coverslips were floated off in Probe Wash Buffer (PWB, 50% formamide, 5 x SSC, 9 mM citric acid pH 6.0, 0.1% Tween-20, 50 μg/ml heparin), then washed in 75% PWB/25% SSCT (5 x SSC, 0.1% Tween-20), 50% PWB/50% SSCT, 25% PWB/75% SSCT, 100% SSCT for 15 min each at 37 °C. This was followed by 5 min at room temperature in SSCT. Slides were incubated in 200 μL of Amplification Buffer (provided by the company) for 30 min at room temperature. Alexa fluor-conjugated DNA hairpins were denatured for 90 s at 95 °C then allowed to cool for at least 30 min in the dark at room temperature. Hairpins were added to 100 μL amplification buffer, applied to slides, and incubated overnight at room temperature. The following day, slides were washed in SSCT containing 1 ng/mL DAPI for 30 min at room temperature, then SSCT for 30 min at room temperature, followed by a final 5 min in SSCT at room temperature. Prolong Glass Antifade Medium (Thermofisher) was added to each slide and then coverslipped. Sections were imaged on a confocal microscope (Zeiss 710) using a 20 X objective.

### FISH quantification

Image quantification was performed using CellProfiler v4.0.4 (Stirling et al., 2021). DAPI-stained nuclei were first identified using the ClassifyPixels-Unet module. Areas corresponding to cells were estimated by extending nuclei boundaries by five pixels. Then signal puncta for each channel were identified and their intensities were measured. For each cell and each channel, we calculated the summed signal intensity of overlapping puncta divided by the cell area. To test for significant differences in gene expression between hearing and deaf birds, a linear mixed effects model was fit using function lmer from R package lmerTest v3.1–3 (Kuznetsova et al., 2017) for each target gene and brain region as ‘intensity ~ condition + (1|bird)’ where ‘condition’ is contra or ipsi and ‘(1|bird)’ is the per-bird grouping factor. p-values were obtained by comparing this model with a reduced model ‘intensity ~ (1|bird)’ using ANOVA.

Reviewer #1 (Recommendations for the authors):

I have no concerns with the data or the analysis, but just one question that the authors may want to consider discussing. Especially in the case of gene expression changes in the interneurons following deafening or in RA following LMAN lesions, could the gene expression changes the authors see primarily result from a decrease in neuronal firing? I have only a small number of comments/questions for the authors:

Major comments

– What is the rationale for including 3 time points post-deafening, given that time post-deafening isn't explicitly considered in most of the analyses of gene expression changes? Are the deaf and hearing birds that overlap in Dkl values those that were sacrificed at the earliest post-procedure timepoint (and that were subsequently excluded from gene expression analyses)? I am not suggesting that the authors change the design or perform additional experiments, but it would be helpful for the reader to more clearly explain the rationale behind including 3 post-procedure time points.

– Can we rule out the possibility that changes in gene expression are due to song destabilization vs. the complete absence of auditory input? Would the authors expect to observe similar changes in gene expression if an alternate method were used that disrupted song stability but preserved hearing (ts nerve cut, etc.)? Conversely, I'm curious what the authors think they would see if they combined bilateral LMAN lesions with deafening (a combination of manipulations that should block song degradation but will still abolish hearing). Again, I'm not suggesting that the authors would perform these additional experiments, but perhaps an expanded discussion of these possibilities added to the discussion would be of interest to readers.

– What is the significance of the relationship of pre-procedure singing rate on LMAN gene expression (measured 9-14 days later; Supplemental Figure 3-1B)? I'm unclear on why singing rates so far in the past would relate LMAN gene expression measured days/weeks later. This is confusing/interesting, particularly given that LMAN gene expression seems much more weakly related to the pre-euthanasia singing rates.

Reviewer #3 (Recommendations for the authors):

The manuscript is extremely well written, the figures are clear and visually compelling, and the existing analysis is reasonable and rigorous. The code is available via GitHub, and methodological details including reagent sources are sufficient. A minor suggestion would be to clarify instances of "described above" (example: line 644) as there is a lot of information here and many things could have been previous. Addressing the outstanding questions outlined in the Public Review would increase the impact of this study, as it would deepen some of the analysis and connect potential mechanisms to long-standing data in the songbird system, and tighten the relationship between the current findings and behavioral outcomes.

results.result: The authors developed SLCR-seq, a novel gene expression profiling method combining laser capture microdissection with single-cell RNA-seq protocols, producing high-quality RNA (RIN=9.1±0.5) and generating 598 samples from spatially-defined brain regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C58-C61 describe the development and validation of SLCR-seq with specific technical metrics (RNA quality, yield, sample numbers) supported by data in Figure 2 and Methods. The method is well-characterized with appropriate quality controls.

results.result: Deafening 9 adult male Bengalese finches (with 9 sham controls) caused gradual song quality decay over several days, with increased syllable noisiness, while sham surgery induced minimal song change.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C34 describe the experimental design and behavioral outcomes supported by Figure 1 data and citations to prior literature. Sample sizes, controls, and behavioral metrics are clearly documented with statistical comparisons.

results.result: Deafening increased fundamental frequency variability (CV increased 57±18% by days 7-9) while sham surgery showed no change, indicating both structural shifts and decreased stereotypy in song.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C42 are supported by quantitative data in Figure 1J-K with statistical tests. The interpretation that deafening affects both song structure and variability is well-supported by the data and consistent with prior literature (C41).

results.result: Deafening preferentially altered gene expression in song regions versus surrounding areas, with RA and Area X showing the largest changes (14 up/11 down in RA, 15 up/16 down in Area X at adjusted p<0.1).
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C8, C73-C76 are supported by differential expression analysis in Figure 3D-E using appropriate statistical methods (voom/limma with adjusted p-values). The regional specificity and gene counts are clearly documented.

results.result: Genes altered by deafening are associated with synaptic transmission, neuronal spines, and neuromodulation, with pathway enrichment varying across song regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C11, C86-C88 are supported by gene set enrichment analysis in Figure 3H using Gene Ontology terms. The analysis appropriately identifies biological pathways and is consistent with prior morphological studies (C88-C89).

results.result: Top upregulated genes in RA include PRKCB (previously shown upregulated after deafening), STMN1, CD24, and LPL; top downregulated genes include CRHBP, SST, and IGF2, all with roles in plasticity.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C78, C82-C83 identify specific differentially expressed genes supported by Figure 3E data and citations to prior literature establishing their functional roles. PRKCB upregulation replicates prior findings (C78), providing validation.

results.result: Deafening-induced gene expression changes show bias toward glutamatergic neurons and Pvalb/Sst-class GABAergic interneurons, with downregulated genes (CRHBP, SST, NPY, CHGB) biased toward Sst/Pvalb interneurons in RA.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C13, C99-C102 are supported by cell type specificity analysis in Figure 5 integrating SLCR-seq with single-cell data. The analysis appropriately uses cell type markers and specificity scores to identify cellular biases.

results.result: Cell type marker genes showed no significant differences between high and low Song DKL conditions, indicating expression changes reflect altered gene expression within cell types rather than changes in cell type abundance.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C104 are supported by analysis in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C comparing marker gene expression to random gene sets. This control appropriately addresses whether observed biases reflect compositional changes versus within-cell-type expression changes.

results.result: Connected song regions showed correlated gene expression that was reduced in deafened versus hearing birds, with specific examples including decorrelation of BDNF (LMAN-RA) and PPARG (LMAN-Area X).
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C16, C113-C115 are supported by inter-region correlation analysis in Figure 6 using appropriate statistical methods (permutation tests). The differential correlation analysis identifies specific genes with altered coordination between regions.

results.result: Song destabilization-associated differential gene expression was more similar between song regions than between song/non-song pairs or non-song regions, indicating a common transcriptional response specific to the song system.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C85 are supported by hypergeometric test analysis in Figure 3F-G comparing overlap of top differentially expressed genes. The statistical approach appropriately tests for greater-than-expected similarity between song regions.

results.result: Gene-gene correlation network analysis identified modules with coordinated expression changes during song destabilization, with segregation of up/downregulated genes and preservation of modules across song regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C94 are supported by MEGENA network analysis in Figure 4 with appropriate statistical validation (permutation tests for module significance, preservation scores). The approach identifies biologically meaningful gene modules.

results.result: Module M74, enriched for secreted neuropeptides (CRHBP, SST, CHGB), was the top downregulated module; upregulated modules were enriched for developmental and gene regulation genes (PBX1, NR2F2, ZHX3, ANKRD11).
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C96, C135 are supported by module analysis and gene set enrichment in Figure 4F-G. The identification of specific hub genes and pathway enrichments is well-documented with appropriate statistical thresholds.

results.result: Inter-region gene expression correlations reflected known anatomical connectivity, with song nuclei showing highest correlation with paired non-song regions and with regions in the same pathway (SMP or AFP).
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C109 are supported by correlation analysis in Figure 6A-B. The observation that gene expression correlations reflect anatomical connectivity provides validation of the approach and biological insight.

results.result: Cluster 3 genes showed correlated expression among pallial song nuclei (HVC-RA, LMAN-RA) and were enriched for activity-dependent genes and signaling receptor binding, including CRHBP, NR4A3, and NRN1.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C112 are supported by clustering and enrichment analysis in Figure 6C-E. The identification of activity-dependent genes with coordinated expression across regions is biologically plausible and well-supported.

results.result: LMAN, a forebrain afferent of RA required for deafening-induced plasticity, when lesioned had the largest effect on gene groups also affected by deafening, with lesions reducing song variability and preventing deafening-induced destabilization.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C20, C116-C120 are supported by prior literature citations and data in Figure 7. The role of LMAN in song plasticity is well-established, and the comparison of lesion effects with deafening effects is appropriate.

results.result: Five birds received unilateral LMAN lesions; lesions did not grossly alter song or Song DKL compared to hearing birds. After 16 days, 91 SLCR-seq libraries were generated from multiple brain regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C121-C125 describe the experimental design and behavioral outcomes supported by Figure 7—figure supplement 1. The unilateral lesion approach appropriately provides within-bird controls.

results.result: RA showed the greatest expression changes between ipsilateral and contralateral sides to LMAN lesion (35 down, 40 up, adjusted p<0.1), with upregulated genes enriched for immune response and downregulated genes enriched for activity-dependent and homeostasis genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C128-C131 are supported by differential expression analysis in Figure 7C-E. The within-bird comparison appropriately controls for individual variation, and the enrichment patterns are biologically interpretable.

results.result: Modules upregulated with song destabilization had lower expression ipsilateral to LMAN lesion and vice versa, except M74 (enriched for neuropeptides including CRHBP, SST) which was reduced in both conditions, possibly reflecting sensitivity to altered neural activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C132-C134, C136 are supported by module comparison in Figure 7F-H. The inverse relationship between deafening and lesion effects is well-documented, though the mechanistic interpretation (C136) is speculative and appropriately qualified.

results.result: Upregulated genes following LMAN lesion were expressed in microglia and astrocytes (with increased microglia markers suggesting increased abundance), while downregulated genes were expressed in glutamatergic and MGE-derived GABAergic neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C137-C139 are supported by cell type analysis in Figure 7—figure supplement 2D-F. The glial response is consistent with injury response, though the interpretation of increased microglia abundance (C138) is inferential.

results.result: SLCR-seq data segregated into three clusters (arcopallium, nidopallium, striatum) consistent with developmental origins, with song/non-song subdivision. SLC17A6 depletion in striatum is consistent with scarcity of excitatory neurons. Expression values corresponded with in situ hybridization.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C67 validate SLCR-seq by showing expected anatomical clustering (Figure 2D), appropriate marker gene expression (Figure 2E), and correspondence with ISH data (Figure 2F, supplement). These validations support the technical quality of the method.

results.result: Song DKL, measuring song change from baseline, was significantly higher in deafened (0.52±0.085) versus hearing birds (0.14±0.041, p=5e-4). Singing rates did not differ significantly between groups.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C69, C72 are supported by data in Figure 3A-B with appropriate statistical tests. The Song DKL metric is validated by prior work (Mets and Brainard, 2018), and controlling for singing rate is methodologically sound.

results.result: Loss of peripheral sensory input drives a distributed gene expression response throughout sensorimotor circuitry and identifies candidate molecular and cellular mechanisms supporting stability and plasticity of learned motor skills.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C20 represent the main conclusions supported by the circuit-wide analysis throughout the manuscript. The distributed response is documented across multiple song regions with identification of specific genes, pathways, and cell types.

results.result: Expression differences in RA following LMAN lesions were broadly inverse to those following deafening, suggesting loss of LMAN establishes a transcriptional state characteristic of reduced plasticity.
results.evaluation: Claims C183-C184 are supported by comparison in Figure 7F-G showing inverse module responses. The interpretation (C184) is appropriately qualified as a suggestion and is consistent with LMAN's known role in plasticity.

results.result: Sensory feedback is required for stable motor skill execution; its loss disrupts motor performance in both birdsong and human speech, with age-dependent effects suggesting similar mechanisms of vocal stabilization.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C21, C140-C143 establish the broader context supported by citations to prior literature. These claims appropriately frame the study's motivation and relevance to human speech, though they represent background knowledge rather than novel findings.

results.result: Songbird courtship song is a learned, highly structured vocalization that serves as a model for skilled behavior. Adult finch song is crystallized (extraordinarily consistent) but is destabilized by deafening or modified auditory feedback.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C5, C22-C27 describe established knowledge about the birdsong system supported by citations to prior literature. These claims appropriately establish the experimental model and are well-supported by the field.

results.result: The song system comprises four primary telencephalic nuclei (HVC, RA, LMAN, Area X) organized into the song motor pathway (HVC-RA) and anterior forebrain pathway (Area X-LMAN-DLM), with each nucleus embedded in larger anatomical domains.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C57 describe the anatomy and organization of the song system, supported by established knowledge and citations. This anatomical framework is essential for interpreting the results and is well-documented in the field.

results.result: Adult birdsong features vary slightly from rendition-to-rendition; this variability is generated by central forebrain mechanisms, modulated by social context, and is an actively regulated component of birdsong.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C38 describe established knowledge about song variability supported by citations to prior literature. This background appropriately motivates the analysis of variability changes following deafening.

results.result: Singing influences gene expression in the song system, and recent singing influences song plasticity and variability.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C71 cite prior literature establishing that singing affects gene expression and plasticity. This background appropriately justifies controlling for singing rate in the regression analysis.

results.result: SLCR-seq data were integrated with previously generated single-cell RNA-seq data from HVC and RA, which showed high transcriptional similarity between songbird and mammalian neuronal classes.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C98 describe the integration approach and cite prior work (Colquitt et al., 2021) establishing cross-species similarities. This integration appropriately enables cell type analysis of the SLCR-seq data.

results.result: Birds lack interhemispheric forebrain connections, with no direct connectivity between song system nuclei across hemispheres.
results.evaluation: Claims C126-C127 describe established anatomical knowledge supported by citations. This fact appropriately justifies the within-bird control design for the unilateral LMAN lesion experiment.

results.result: Prior studies identified various circuit, cellular, and molecular mechanisms contributing to deafening-induced song destabilization, including changes to spine stability, synapse densities, LMAN tuning responses, and HVC projection neuron properties.
results.evaluation: Claims C144-C147 summarize prior literature on mechanisms of song destabilization. These claims appropriately establish the existing knowledge base and motivate the circuit-wide transcriptomic approach.

results.result: RA lies at the nexus of motor and plasticity pathways and is a major locus of neural plasticity. Prior work showed deafening increases synapse/spine densities and lengths in RA and decreases spine stability in HVC neurons projecting to Area X.
results.evaluation: Claims C148-C153 cite prior literature establishing RA's role in plasticity and morphological changes following deafening. This background appropriately contextualizes the gene expression findings.

results.result: Several upregulated genes in RA (STMN1, CD24, LPL) have established roles in synaptic plasticity, with knockout studies in mice showing impaired LTP, memory, and synaptic function.
results.evaluation: Claims C154-C160 cite prior literature establishing functional roles of specific genes. This discussion appropriately connects the gene expression findings to known molecular mechanisms of plasticity.

results.result: Neuropeptide signaling has powerful effects on neural circuit activity and plasticity. CRHBP modulates the CRH signaling pathway, which affects LTP, neuronal excitability, and spine dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claims C161-C163 cite prior literature on neuropeptide function. This discussion appropriately interprets the downregulation of neuropeptide genes in the context of known signaling mechanisms.

results.result: RA glutamatergic neurons are similar to mammalian layer 5 extratelencephalic neurons. Song system interneurons are similar to mammalian neocortical interneurons. Song learning refines connectivity between RA projection neurons and Pvalb-like interneurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C164-C168 cite prior literature establishing cross-species similarities and developmental refinement of inhibitory circuits. This discussion appropriately contextualizes the cell type-specific expression findings.

results.result: Sst/Pvalb-biased genes affected by deafening are activity-dependent secreted neuropeptides, suggesting reduced activity in these populations. SST and CRHBP act to inhibit neural activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C169-C171 integrate the data with prior literature on activity-dependent gene expression and neuropeptide function. The inference of reduced interneuron activity (C170) is appropriately qualified and biologically plausible.

results.result: In mammalian motor cortex and hippocampus, Sst/Pvalb interneuron synapses are modulated during motor learning, with reduced Sst input and low Pvalb activity associated with plasticity. Similar changes occur in auditory cortex after deafening, suggesting reduced inhibition is a key component of plasticity.
results.evaluation: Claims C172-C176 cite prior literature on inhibitory plasticity in mammals. The inference that reduced inhibition is a conserved plasticity mechanism (C176) is appropriately qualified and supported by convergent evidence.

results.result: Regions with direct projections showed higher gene expression correlations than unconnected regions. Genes correlated across pallial song regions (HVC, RA, LMAN) were enriched for activity-dependent genes and secreted neuropeptides.
results.evaluation: Claims C177-C178 are supported by correlation and enrichment analysis in Figure 6. The observation that connectivity predicts expression correlation provides biological validation and mechanistic insight.

results.result: LMAN lesions altered gene expression specifically in RA (its primary efferent) but not other regions. HVC and LMAN converge onto RA with distinct roles. Prior studies examined how disrupting these inputs affects RA physiology, but little is known about molecular effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C179-C182 are supported by the lesion data (Figure 7C-D) and citations to prior literature. The observation of target-specific effects validates the approach and identifies a knowledge gap appropriately addressed by this study.

results.result: Bilateral LMAN lesions before cochlear removal prevent deafening-induced song destabilization (established by prior work).
results.evaluation: Claim C185 cites prior literature establishing this manipulation. This is mentioned as a suggested follow-up experiment to further dissect the relationship between LMAN activity and deafening-induced plasticity.
